To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dietary fat and energy density increase body weight and feed efficiency in turkeys, but only when birds are exposed to a high environmental temperature.
the responses of weight gain, feed conversion, and carcass composition to dietary energy sources are affected by environmental temperature.

dietary fat is the most effective dietary source of energy for weight gain in turkeys at both low and high temperatures, whereas dietary carbohydrate (glucose) is more effective at the low than at the high temperature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of dietary energy sources (carbohydrates and fat) on the growth performance of turkeys kept in two different environmental temperatures (10 and 27C).
interactions of dietary carbohydrates and fat with the environment on growth and carcass fat deposition in turkeys.
the effects of environmental temperature and dietary composition on the performance and carcass fat deposition of turkeys.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the response of turkeys to energy sources and to environmental temperature are not independent of each other.
dietary carbohydrates and fat interact with environmental temperature to influence the performance of turkeys in different ways, depending upon the mode of dietary energy supplementation.
dietary energy sources interacted with environmental temperature to influence weight gain, feed intake, and carcass composition in turkeys.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dietary energy sources interacted with temperature to produce differential responses in weight gain, feed utilization, and carcass composition.

the responses of weight gain, feed conversion efficiency and carcass fat to dietary energy density are greater in birds kept at 27 C than in those kept at 10 C, and that the response to dietary carbohydrates is greater at 10 C than at 27 C.
the response of weight gain to dietary fat is more temperature dependent than that of feed efficiency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the response of turkeys to dietary energy sources is influenced by environmental temperature and that the response to energy sources is not always the same.
turkeys are able to adjust their feed intake and energy expenditure to compensate for changes in dietary energy density.
the effect of dietary energy source on performance of turkeys is temperature dependent.
